There are three different methods of transfer of heat. For example; when one end of a metallic
rod is heated, the other end also gets heated. When a liquid in a vessel is heated from the
bottom, the upper surface of the liquid also gets heated. We receive the heat from a very hot
object, and from the sun directly.

Transfer of heat due to molecular vibrations in a solid as in the case of a metallic rod is called conduction. Transfer of heat due to actual molecular translation in fluid is called convection. Boiling of water is an example of convection. Transfer of heat without the support of any material medium is called radiation e.g., receiving heat from the sun.

12.2 Conduction

When one end of a solid is heated, atoms in this hotter region vibrate with greater amplitude and have more kinetic energy than the neighboring atoms in the colder region. The atoms in the hotter region collide with the neighboring atoms in the colder region. During the process, hotter molecules give up some energy to colder molecules. The same phenomena occur between each set of neighboring atoms and the process continues up to the next end. This method of heat transfer is called conduction. Conduction also takes place between two different bodies if they are in thermal contact.

Therefore, conduction is defined as the process of transfer of heat from one point to another point of a body, carried out by means of collisions between rapidly vibrating atoms in the hotter region and slowly vibrating atoms in the colder region. There is no

actual transfer of particles during conduction.
Material medium is required for the conduction. Molecular collisions enhanced by molecular vibrations are the means of conduction of heat.

The ability of anybody to conduct heat is measured in terms of thermal conductivity. Generally, metals have a high value of thermal conductivity. Therefore, metals are called good conductors of heat. The materials which do not conduct heat are called bad conductors. For example; paper, air, plastic, wood, etc.

Examples and Applications of Thermal Conduction in Our Daily Life 1. Two thin jackets are warmer than a single jacket of the same thickness because the air particles trapped between two jackets minimize the conduction. 2. The Eskimo houses are double-walled so that the air trapped between two walls behaves as a bad conductor, and prevents the flow of heat from inside to outside. 3. In cold countries, windows have two panes of glass with a thin layer of air in between. 4. Thick walls are constructed in cold storage rooms. 5. To remove a stopper fitted tightly to the bottle, the neck is immersed in warm water and gently heated. The glass neck being a bad conductor expands but does not conduct heat to the stopper. So that the stopper can be removed easily. 6. Sauce pans, hot water buckets, kettles, etc. are made of metal but their handles are of wooden or ebonite or Bakelite so that heat from utensils cannot conduct to hand. 7. Woolen clothes have fine pores filled with air. Air and wool both are bad conductors of heat. So that the flow of heat from the body to outside the atmosphere is prevented. Therefore, woolen clothes provide good insulation and keep our body warm in winter. 8. In a thermos bottle, a vacuum is created between two surfaces to avoid the transfer of heat due to conduction. 9. We feel iron chairs colder than wooden chairs in winter. 10. Ice is packed in saw-dust inside double-walled ice box wrapped in gunny bags to prevent from melting. 11. Quilts are filled with fluffy cotton. Cotton can trap air in its pores. Both cotton and air are bad conductors and provide good insulation. As a result, the flow of heat is prevented, and keeps our body warm. A newly built quilt can trap more air as it contains more pores than an old one. Therefore, a newly built quilt is warmer than an old one.
